Case Vignette: "Lieutenant Commander D."

Lieutenant Commander D. is a 34-year-old married Navy officer who presents for therapy at the urging of his wife. He has been on shore duty for the past eighteen months, following a decade of active sea service. In our sessions, he sits upright, hands clasped, and speaks with the measured precision of someone used to giving briefings, but his eyes betray a constant scanning of the room-checking exits, checking the ceiling, checking the window.

The trauma happened three years ago, during a humanitarian assistance mission in the Pacific. His ship was anchored off a small island nation when a Category 5 super typhoon, which had been forecast to pass well north, made an unexpected, violent turn directly toward the fleet. In his words, the warning came "too late to run." He was the officer of the deck when the order came to get the ship underway. He remembers the radar screen turning solid red, the wind screaming at 160 knots, and the ship heaving at its anchor chain like a toy. The worst part, he says, was not the storm itself-it was the aftermath. The ship survived, but the island was gone. Entire villages were simply erased. For seventy-two hours, he led search-and-recovery teams through mud and debris, pulling bodies from what used to be schools and homes. He found a child's shoe, still tied, floating in a lagoon. He still sees that shoe.

When he returned home, he told his wife he was fine. He told his command he was fine. He was a Navy officer-he was trained to be fine. But he was not fine. He began waking at 3:17 AM every night, the exact time the typhoon's eye passed over his position. He would be drenched in sweat, convinced he could hear the wind. He started driving the long way to work to avoid a bridge that crosses a wide river, because the sight of fast-moving water makes his chest tighten and his vision tunnel. At home, he has become irritable, snapping at his wife for small things-a dish left in the sink, a door left open. He has stopped going to the gym, stopped calling his friends from the ship. He says he feels "dead inside," like the part of him that used to feel joy or excitement or even sadness has been scooped out.

His wife reports that he has become hypervigilant. He checks the weather forecast obsessively, multiple times a day. He has installed a backup generator, bought three months of non-perishable food, and insists on having a "go-bag" in the trunk of his car. When a thunderstorm passed through last spring, he spent the entire night standing in the living room, staring at the sky through the sliding glass door, refusing to sit down or speak. He could not explain why he was doing it. He just knew he had to watch.

At work, he is competent but withdrawn. He avoids the ship's damage control training exercises, finding excuses to be in meetings. The smell of diesel fuel and the sound of alarms-even a fire drill-send him into a state of numbed detachment. He describes it as "watching myself from across the room." He has not told his commanding officer about any of this. He fears it would end his career. He says, "I'm supposed to be the guy who stays calm when everything is falling apart. And I did. I was calm. But now I can't stop falling apart."

His PCL-5 score is 33, indicating clinically significant PTSD symptoms. He endorses intrusive memories, nightmares, intense psychological distress at reminders, avoidance of both internal and external cues, negative beliefs about himself and the world, anhedonia, hypervigilance, and an exaggerated startle response. He does not endorse suicidal ideation, but he does say, with a hollow laugh, that he sometimes wishes he could just "turn off the movie that keeps playing in my head."

He is here because his wife told him she cannot watch him disappear anymore. He does not know if talking about it will help. He is not sure he wants to be helped. But he has shown up.
